question_text: Explain the role of geographical factors towards the development of Ancient India.
topic: Geography in the making of ancient India
topics: Geography in the making of ancient India
customKeyPointers: Rivers, soil and a monsoon made the first surplus
Mountains and seas set the limits of kingdoms and of trade
Geography shaped India; it did not write its history alone

points.text: Ancient India grew where the land made a surplus possible.
The Indus and the Ganga plains, alluvial soil and a seasonal rain supported dense farming, towns and a state that could tax grain.
The Himalaya, the oceans and the passes decided invasion, pilgrimage and trade, while iron, forests and coasts fed crafts and ports.
Geography set the stage. Kings, faith and technology decided what was built on it.

question_text: What was the difference between Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore in their approach towards education and nationalism?
topic: Gandhi and Tagore on education and nationalism
topics: Gandhi and Tagore on education and nationalism
customKeyPointers: Gandhi wanted a village school tied to work and swaraj
Tagore wanted a free mind, art and the world, not only the nation
Both rejected colonial schooling, and they did not reject it for the same end

points.text: Both men refused the colonial classroom. They wanted different human beings to come out of the refusal.
Gandhi tied education to the mother tongue, craft and a village nationalism that would spin, clean and govern itself.
Tagore feared a narrow nation. His school opened the child to nature, art and the world, and he warned Gandhi that a charkha is not a whole education.
Gandhi educated for swaraj. Tagore educated for a free person who could belong to a nation without being shut inside it.

question_text: Bring out the socio-economic effects of the introduction of railways in different countries of the world.
topic: Railways and socio-economic change
topics: Railways and socio-economic change
customKeyPointers: Railways shrank distance and enlarged the market
They built nations and they also extracted colonies
The same machine integrated some people and displaced others

points.text: The railway was an economic machine that rearranged society wherever it was laid.
In industrial countries it created a national market, standard time, commuting and a working class that could move.
In colonies it moved troops, grain and raw material to ports, often before it served the people who lived beside the line.
Railways connected the world and, at the same time, decided who that connection was for.

question_text: Discuss the consequence of Climate change on the food security in tropical countries.
topic: Climate change and tropical food security
topics: Climate change and tropical food security
customKeyPointers: Heat, flood and a failed rain hit the tropics first
Yields fall where farmers already have thin margins
Food security fails as access, not only as a harvest

points.text: Tropical countries grow much of the world's food and have the least room for a hotter climate.
Erratic monsoon, heat stress, flood and salt in coastal fields cut the yield of rice, maize and millets.
A smaller harvest raises prices, and the poor lose access even when some grain is still in the market.
The consequence is hunger with a climate cause, and it falls on the countries least responsible for the warming.

question_text: Why is the world today confronted with a crisis of availability of and access to freshwater resources?
topic: The freshwater crisis of availability and access
topics: The freshwater crisis of availability and access
customKeyPointers: The stock of usable water is uneven and overdrawn
Pollution turns available water into unusable water
Access fails where pipes, rights and money are missing

points.text: The crisis is not that the planet has no water. It is that usable water is in the wrong place, and many people cannot reach it.
Aquifers are mined, rivers are dammed and diverted, and a growing city, farm and industry drink the same finite stock.
Sewage and industry spoil what remains, while the poor pay more for a tanker than the rich pay for a tap.
Availability is a physical shortage. Access is a political one. Both are now present together.

question_text: How are the fjords formed? Why do they constitute some of the most picturesque areas of the world?
topic: How fjords are formed
topics: How fjords are formed
customKeyPointers: A fjord is a glacial valley drowned by the sea
Ice cut a deep U-shape that water later filled
Steep walls and still water are the exposed work of ice

points.text: A fjord is a long, steep-sided sea inlet that a glacier cut and the sea then occupied.
Valley glaciers over-deepened a river valley into a U-shape, often below sea level, and left a shallow threshold at the mouth.
When the ice melted, the sea entered. The walls, the waterfalls and the dark water are what the visitor calls picturesque.
The view is famous because the glacier removed everything except the rock it could not.

question_text: Why is the South-West Monsoon called 'Purvaiya' (easterly) in Bhojpur Region? How has this directional seasonal wind system influenced the cultural ethos of the region?
topic: Purvaiya and the Bhojpur cultural ethos
topics: Purvaiya and the Bhojpur cultural ethos
customKeyPointers: The same monsoon arrives in Bhojpur from the east
Local direction, not the ocean source, gave it the name Purvaiya
The wind entered song, farming and the calendar

points.text: In Bhojpur the south-west monsoon is called Purvaiya because, by the time it reaches the region, it blows from the east.
The Bay of Bengal branch curves and enters Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh as an easterly, bringing the rain the fields wait for.
Songs, sowing dates and the mood of the season took their name from that wind, so a direction became part of the ethos.
The monsoon is a weather system. Purvaiya is what a region made of the direction it arrives from.

question_text: Do you think marriage as a sacrament is losing its value in Modern India?
topic: Marriage as a sacrament in modern India
topics: Marriage as a sacrament in modern India
customKeyPointers: The sacrament treated marriage as a rite, not a contract
Choice, law and divorce have made it more negotiable
The rite survives; the unquestioned duty does not

points.text: Marriage in India was long treated as a sacrament, a rite that joined families rather than a contract two adults could exit.
Education, urban work, love marriage and a legal right of divorce have made the bond look more like a choice.
The wedding ritual is still lavish. What has weakened is the idea that the bond cannot be questioned.
The sacrament has not vanished. It now shares the ground with a companionate and a legal marriage.

question_text: Explain why suicide among young women is increasing in Indian society.
topic: Suicide among young women
topics: Suicide among young women
customKeyPointers: Early marriage, violence and a denied education sit close to the numbers
Exam pressure and a public failure add a newer layer
A death is counted; the isolation before it is not

points.text: A rising suicide rate among young women is a social fact, not only a private illness.
Domestic violence, early marriage, dowry pressure and the blocking of study or work leave many women with no acceptable exit.
In cities and campuses, academic rank, a broken relationship and social media shame add a public kind of failure.
The increase points to a society that still polices young women and offers too few places where distress can be said aloud.

question_text: Child cuddling is now being replaced by mobile phones. Discuss its impact on the socialization of children.
topic: Mobile phones and the socialisation of children
topics: Mobile phones and the socialisation of children
customKeyPointers: Socialisation needs a responding adult, not a glowing screen
The phone soothes the child and skips the relationship
The device is a tool; using it as a parent is the harm

points.text: A phone can quiet a child. It cannot do the work of being held.
Early socialisation is learnt in eye contact, refusal, comfort and play with a person who answers back.
A screen gives stimulus without that answer, so speech, attention and the habit of waiting for another person grow thin.
The phone has not replaced childhood. It has replaced the adult in the room, and that is the impact.

question_text: What are the main features of Vedic society and religion? Do you think some of the features are still prevailing in Indian society?
topic: Vedic society
topics: Vedic society
customKeyPointers: Vedic society was pastoral, patriarchal and arranged by varna
Religion moved from outdoor ritual toward a more inward search
Some forms remain, and they do not remain unchanged

points.text: Vedic society was a cattle-keeping, Sanskrit-speaking order organised around the sacrifice and a graded status.
The family was patriarchal. Varna sorted work and rank. The king protected the sacrifice, and the ritualist held knowledge the ordinary householder did not.
Early religion was hymnal and fire-centred. Later layers added philosophy, the idea of karma, and a turn inward that the Upanishads record.
What still shows is a household rite, a priest at a life-cycle ceremony, and a status that people deny in public and practise in marriage.
The features that prevail have been edited by caste reform, law and a different economy. They prevail as habit, not as the Vedic world itself.

question_text: What were the major technological changes introduced during the Sultanate period? How did those technological changes influence the Indian society?
topic: Sultanate technology
topics: Sultanate technology
customKeyPointers: The new tools included the wheel, the arch, paper and a geared water lift
They changed building, cloth, irrigation and the written record
The influence was urban and craft-based before it was rural

points.text: The Sultanate brought a set of tools that altered how India built, spun, lifted water and kept a record.
The spinning wheel, the drawloom, paper, the true arch and dome, and the Persian wheel or saqiya are the changes usually named.
Cloth became cheaper and more varied. Paper enlarged the chancery and the copyist. The arch changed the skyline of mosque, tomb and fort. The water-lift extended irrigation.
New crafts made new urban groups. They did not abolish the village order, and many tools were adopted slowly and unevenly.
The social influence was a wider market, a written state and a changed city, not a single revolution in the countryside.

question_text: How did the colonial rule affect the tribals in India and what was the tribal response to the colonial oppression?
topic: Colonial rule and the tribal response
topics: Colonial rule and the tribal response
customKeyPointers: Forest, land and tax were taken out of tribal control
Outsiders entered as moneylender, trader and contractor
The response was revolt, migration and a religious renewal

points.text: Colonial rule reached the tribes mainly as a new owner of the forest and a new claimant of their labour.
Reserved forests, a cash rent, bans on shifting cultivation and on customary use, and the arrival of the diku broke the old subsistence.
Many were pushed into plantation, mine and bonded work. Others lost land to a settler who had a paper the tribe did not.
The reply was revolt: Santhal, Munda under Birsa, Bhil, Kol and others, often led by a figure who joined a religious promise to a demand for the old land.
The tribal response was not a footnote to the national movement. It was a defence of a forest economy the colony had decided to administer.

question_text: Comment on the resource potentials of the long coastline of India and highlight the status of natural hazard preparedness in these areas.
topic: Coastal resources and hazard preparedness
topics: Coastal resources and hazard preparedness
customKeyPointers: The coast is fisheries, ports, energy and a living shore
The same length is exposed to cyclone, surge and erosion
Warning has improved faster than the last mile

points.text: India's long coastline is a resource and a hazard line at the same time.
Fisheries, ports, offshore energy, salt, tourism and a dense coastal population are the potential.
Cyclone, storm surge, tsunami, erosion and a rising sea are the hazards, and they fall on the same districts that hold the resource.
Forecasting and evacuation have improved since the great cyclones. Shelters, mangrove buffers, enforcing the setback and a plan for the poorest hamlet are still uneven.
Preparedness is no longer the absence of a warning. It is whether the last village can act on one.

question_text: Identify and discuss the factors responsible for diversity of natural vegetation in India. Assess the significance of wildlife sanctuaries in rain forest regions of India.
topic: Vegetation diversity and rainforest sanctuaries
topics: Vegetation diversity and rainforest sanctuaries
customKeyPointers: Climate, relief, soil and a long human use make the diversity
Rainforest is the wet end of that range
A sanctuary holds species that a timber line will not

points.text: India's vegetation runs from alpine pasture to rainforest because the land itself runs through many climates.
Rainfall, temperature, altitude, soil and the length of the dry season sort the types. Human clearing, fire and grazing have sorted them further.
Rainforests of the Western Ghats, the Northeast and the islands hold endemics, watersheds and a stock of species found nowhere else.
A sanctuary there limits logging, a plantation and a road, and it keeps a corridor that a reserved forest on paper often does not.
Sanctuaries matter because the rainforest's value is the whole stand, and that stand does not survive as a calculation of timber.

question_text: Why did human development fail to keep pace with economic development in India?
topic: Human development lagging economic growth
topics: Human development lagging economic growth
customKeyPointers: Growth raised income faster than it raised capability
Health, schooling and nutrition were not the first claim on the surplus
A rising GDP can coexist with a stalled human outcome

points.text: India's income grew faster than the health, learning and nutrition of its people.
Public spending on school, primary care and a child diet stayed thin while growth was led by services that employ the already educated.
Regional and gender gaps meant a state average hid a district where the child was still stunted.
Jobs of poor quality, an informal workforce and a weak local state slowed the conversion of income into capability.
Human development failed to keep pace because growth was not aimed at it, and the institutions that could have aimed it were underbuilt.

question_text: From being a net food importer in 1960, India has emerged as a net food exporter to the world. Provide reasons.
topic: From food importer to food exporter
topics: From food importer to food exporter
subTopics: India as a net food exporter
customKeyPointers: The break was the green revolution, not a single policy
Procurement and irrigation locked the surplus in
A national surplus can still leave a household hungry

points.text: In 1960 India imported grain to avoid a famine. It now exports a surplus of several foods.
High-yielding wheat and rice, irrigation, fertiliser and a public research system created the first dependable surplus.
Procurement, a minimum price and the public stock turned that surplus into a policy, not a one-year accident.
Horticulture, basmati, buffalo meat, fish and sugar widened the export basket beyond the two cereals.
The reasons are technological and institutional. They produced a national surplus, which is not the same thing as food for every household.

question_text: Does urbanization lead to more segregation and/or marginalization of the poor in Indian metropolises?
topic: Urbanisation and the marginalisation of the poor
topics: Urbanisation and the marginalisation of the poor
customKeyPointers: The city sorts people by what they can pay for land
Work pulls the poor in; housing and services push them out
Urbanisation segregates when the plan does not include the worker

points.text: Indian metropolises grow by pulling in labour and then housing that labour at the edge.
Land price, a slum clearance and a gated colony separate the poor from the services, the schools and the jobs they serve.
Informal work, a missing title and a distant resettlement colony make the separation durable.
It is not urbanisation as such. A city that builds rental housing and transport for the worker segregates less.
In the form Indian metros have actually taken, urbanisation has increased both segregation and the marginalisation of the poor.

question_text: Why is caste identity in India both fluid and static?
topic: Caste identity as fluid and static
topics: Caste identity as fluid and static
customKeyPointers: The label sticks; the person can move around it
Migration, education and a new job loosen daily practice
Marriage and politics re-fasten the same label

points.text: Caste in India changes its behaviour without giving up its name.
A person can change occupation, city and party, so the identity looks fluid in work and in public life.
Marriage, surname, a reservation claim and a local vote keep the same identity fixed.
It is fluid in practice and static as a boundary. Both descriptions are true of the same institution.

question_text: Discuss the impact of post-liberal economy on ethnic identity and communalism.
topic: The post-liberal economy, ethnicity and communalism
topics: The post-liberal economy, ethnicity and communalism
customKeyPointers: A market economy unsettled old securities
Identity became a way to claim a share of the new growth
Communalism was not caused by reform alone, but reform fed it

points.text: After 1991 the economy opened, and ethnic and religious identities did not fade. Several of them hardened.
Lost job security, a new middle class and a visible inequality gave people a reason to look for a group that would claim a share.
Competition for education, contracts and a city job was easily narrated as a contest between communities.
Private media and a political party could sell that narration cheaper than before, because the audience was already unsettled.
The post-liberal economy did not invent communalism. It gave ethnic identity a new stake, and communal politics a larger market.
